title: What Node.js is
idea: Node.js is a runtime that lets JavaScript run outside the browser, so you can write servers, tools and scripts in the same language.

analogy.text: JavaScript is a recipe, and a runtime is the kitchen that cooks it. Chrome's kitchen serves a web page; Node's kitchen serves files and network connections.
analogy.breaks: Recipes are portable; code using browser-only objects like `document` is not.

points: Node.js runs your JavaScript with V8, the engine inside Chrome.
Built-in modules such as `fs` and `http` add files and networking.
One thread serves many requests, because async I/O waits happen outside your code.
npm, installed with Node, gives you ready-made packages to reuse.

edges.label: runs on
edges.caption: V8, the engine from Chrome, compiles and runs your JavaScript. On its own it has no file or network access.

edges.label: calls
edges.caption: Your code calls built-in modules: `fs` for files, `http` for servers, `path` for file paths.

edges.label: hands off
edges.caption: Those modules pass slow work, such as reading a file, to libuv, a C library inside Node.

edges.label: asks
edges.caption: libuv asks the operating system for the data, then calls your code back. The event loop page shows how.

code.title: A tiny server
code.caption: Server-side JavaScript. The process stays alive between requests, so `visits` keeps counting. HTTP gets its own chapter.

walk.text: `http` is a built-in module, so there is nothing to install.
`visits` lives outside the handler, so it survives from one request to the next.
The handler runs once per request: add one, then reply with the count.
Port `0` asks the operating system for any free port.
The script calls its own server twice with `fetch`, which Node 20 includes.
Close the server so the script can exit.

pitfalls: Do not run long CPU-heavy loops in a handler; one slow request stalls all others.
Keep important data in a database; variables like `visits` reset when the process restarts.
Do not use browser-only names such as `window` or `document`; Node does not define them.

quiz.q: The counter now lives inside the handler. What do two requests receive?
quiz.why: The handler runs once per request, so `visits` restarts at 0 each time. Outside the handler it lives as long as the process.

takeaway: A Node server is one long-running process, so module-level variables outlive requests.
